persona.name: Hiroshi Tanaka
persona.background: Salaryman father commuting to Tokyo, mother part-time at a supermarket. Watched The Best Ten (TBS) on Thursdays and Yoru no Hit Studio (Fuji TV) with his older sister; taped songs off Bunka Hoso and FM Tokyo onto cassettes; borrowed LPs from the local rental record shop to dub. Bought his first single (Checkers) in 1984.

seeds.song: Anzen Chitai - Wine Red no Kokoro
Dead or Alive - You Spin Me Round (Like a Record)
Cyndi Lauper - Girls Just Want to Have Fun

JP1984A.wouldSay: Namida no Request! Everyone in my class did the Checkers hair. And Wine Red no Kokoro was on Best Ten every week that winter.
missing: Akina Nakamori - Kazari ja Nai no yo Namida wa (1984)
Kyoko Koizumi - Nagisa no Haikara Ningyo (1984)
JP1984A.fake: Little feels fake, but most of the middle is 1980-82, so it drifts to 'early 80s' rather than 1984, and three of the foreign hits were released only in Nov-Dec 1984 and really landed in Japan in 1985.

seeds.song: Mari Iijima - Ai Oboete Imasu ka

JP1984B.wouldSay: Plastic Love? Never heard it on the radio. Ah, Cat's Eye, that one I know from the anime. But who is this Midnight Pretenders?
missing: Anzen Chitai - Wine Red no Kokoro (1983)
Akina Nakamori - Kazari ja Nai no yo Namida wa (1984)
Kyoko Koizumi - Nagisa no Haikara Ningyo (1984)
JP1984B.fake: It opens with the 2010s YouTube city-pop revival canon (Plastic Love, Midnight Pretenders, Just a Joke were album tracks nobody my age heard), then pads with childhood anime themes, and has no foreign hits at all though Wham! and Cyndi Lauper were everywhere.

persona.name: Adebayo Ogunleye
persona.background: Yoruba family; father a federal civil servant, mother a trader at Oyingbo market. Listened to Radio Nigeria and Radio Lagos request shows, watched NTA Lagos, heard records blasted from record stalls and at owambe parties with juju bands; older cousins went to Fela's Shrine; bought 45s and tapes on the street.

seeds.song: Fela Kuti & Africa 70 - Shuffering and Shmiling
Fela Kuti & Africa 70 - Sorrow, Tears and Blood
Fela Kuti & Africa 70 - Water No Get Enemy
Alhaji Garba Leao - Wurin Allah Muki Nema
Alhaji Garba Leao - Sarkin Mallamai Garba Kaita

NG1978A.wouldSay: Fela, Fela, Fela, Fela... yes, Zombie was everywhere after the soldiers burned Kalakuta. But where is Sunny Ade? Where is Obey? This is not what my parents' parties sounded like.
missing: Bongos Ikwue - Still Searching (c.1976, year unsure)
King Sunny Ade & His African Beats - any mid-70s juju side (specific title unsure)
Ebenezer Obey & His Inter-Reformers - any mid-70s juju side (specific title unsure)
NG1978A.fake: It is a Western crate-digger's Nigeria: five Fela tracks back to back, three obscure Hausa reissue tracks and an expatriate drummer's US albums, with no juju, no highlife beyond Sweet Mother and none of the Nigerian pop that actually filled radio.

NG1978B.wouldSay: Ah, Bongos! Still Searching! And Sonny Okosuns, Fire in Soweto, we sang that at school when everybody was talking about South Africa.
missing: King Sunny Ade & His African Beats - any mid-70s juju side (specific title unsure)

NG1978B.fake: Mostly right, but for a Lagos family it is thin on juju (one Obey track whose date I am unsure of) and the year-of-release on The Gambler (Nov 1978) means it only reached Nigeria afterwards.

persona.name: Samira Abdel Fattah
persona.background: Father a schoolteacher, mother at home. Family gathered around the radio for Umm Kulthum's first-Thursday concerts on Idha'at al-Qahira and Sawt al-Arab; saw Abdel Halim and Shadia films at the neighbourhood cinema; patriotic songs at school assemblies; a neighbour had a gramophone with Sono Cairo records.

seeds.song: Mohammed Abdel Wahab - El Watan El Akbar

EG1965A.wouldSay: Amal Hayati, the new one that year, my father would not let anyone speak during it. And Enta Omri, the whole street listened.
missing: Shadia - a mid-60s film song (specific title unsure)
Faiza Ahmed - Ya Imma El Amar Ala El Bab (1950s)
EG1965A.fake: Every track is real and loved, but five of eight are hour-long Umm Kulthum concert pieces, so it plays like a grandparent's tarab evening rather than a teenager's 1965 of film songs, Abdel Halim, Shadia and the light pop on the radio.

EG1965B.wouldSay: Enta Omri, then Ahwak, yes. Al Rabie, my mother's favourite. But Quran recitation in the middle of songs? And this Algerian woman, who is she?
missing: Mohammed Abdel Wahab - El Watan El Akbar (1960)
Shadia - a mid-60s film song (specific title unsure)
EG1965B.fake: The opening is right, but the rest is a museum of Arab music (1940s Asmahan and Abdel Wahab) with token 'world' inserts: a Quran recitation treated as a song, an Algerian rai singer unknown in Cairo, and Indian and Hollywood items of uncertain reach.

persona.name: Andrei Volkov
persona.background: Father a lathe operator at the arms plant, mother a nurse. Watched Pesnya Goda and Goluboy Ogonyok on Central Television, radio Mayak in the kitchen; Melodiya LPs and flexidiscs from Krugozor; older brother copied Vysotsky and Mashina Vremeni onto reel-to-reel from friends; school discotheques played Boney M. and ABBA; 1980 Olympics on TV.

seeds.song: Samotsvety - Uvezu tebya ya v tundru
Smokie - Living Next Door to Alice
Joe Dassin - Et si tu n'existais pas

RU1980A.wouldSay: Povorot! My brother's tape, we wore it out. And then Vsyo mogut koroli, Pugacheva was on TV every New Year.
missing: Lev Leshchenko & Tatyana Antsiferova - Do svidaniya, Moskva (1980)
RU1980A.fake: Almost nothing; the only doubts are that the 'Uvezu tebya ya v tundru' I remember is Kola Beldy's, not Samotsvety's (I am unsure a Samotsvety recording is the famous one), and the 1980 Olympic songs are absent.

seeds.song: Joy Division - Love Will Tear Us Apart

RU1980B.wouldSay: Zykina, Ruslanova, Chaliapin... this is my grandmother's radio, not mine. Where is Pugacheva? Oh, there she is, eighth.
missing: Lev Leshchenko & Tatyana Antsiferova - Do svidaniya, Moskva (1980)

RU1980B.fake: It opens on a folkloric 'eternal Russia' of Zykina, wartime Ruslanova and pre-revolutionary Chaliapin, and ends with Western metal and post-punk (Judas Priest, Devo, Joy Division) that no Soviet teenager in 1980 had heard, instead of the ABBA, Boney M. and Smokie actually played at school discos.
